question: A company has £200m of accumulated tax losses and EBIT of £100m a year. Tax is 25 %. How would you handle that in a DCF?
model_answer_md:
I would keep the operating cash flow clean and treat the losses as a separate asset.

In the cash flow itself, tax EBIT at the full 25 % as usual — £25m a year, giving £75m of NOPAT. That keeps the unlevered cash flow comparable with peers who have no losses.

Then value the losses on their own. At £100m of EBIT a year, the £200m of losses shelters profit for two years, saving £25m of cash tax in each. Discount those two savings at WACC — at 8 %, roughly £23.1m and £21.4m — so about **£44.5m** of present value, added to enterprise value as a distinct line.

The alternative is to model the cash tax directly inside the forecast, showing zero tax for two years and 25 % thereafter. That gives a similar answer but hides the benefit inside the operating cash flow, where it is harder to see and harder to compare.
key_points: Keep the operating UFCF at the full marginal tax rate for comparability
Value the losses separately as a discounted stream of cash tax saved
£200m of losses against £100m EBIT shelters two years at £25m each
Discounted at 8 %: roughly £44.5m of present value
Add it to enterprise value as a distinct asset, not buried in the forecast

follow_ups.question: Why value them separately rather than just modelling a lower tax rate?
follow_ups.answer_md: Three reasons. It keeps the operating cash flow comparable with peer companies that have no losses. It makes a temporary benefit visible as a finite number rather than hiding it inside a blended rate that a reader might mistake for permanent. And it forces you to state the assumptions the value actually depends on — how quickly profits absorb the losses, and whether local rules cap the annual usage, which many jurisdictions do.

follow_ups.question: Would an acquirer get the full value of those losses?
follow_ups.answer_md: Often not. Most tax regimes restrict the use of carried-forward losses after a change of ownership — sometimes capping the annual amount, sometimes disallowing them if the business changes substantially. So in an M&A context the losses are usually worth materially less to a buyer than to the company standing alone, and that gap is a real negotiating point. In a valuation for a sale I would haircut them and flag the assumption.

weak_answer_note: Applying a zero tax rate to the whole forecast, which massively overstates the benefit — the losses are finite. Or ignoring the losses entirely, which understates value. Not knowing that ownership changes can restrict their use is the gap at this level.
